lessons.title: Choose an API style
lessons.intro: So far the course has used one style: resources reached with HTTP methods, often called REST. It is the most common style for public APIs, but not the only one. This module compares it with three others, so that you can recognize them and choose on purpose. The principles from the earlier modules apply to all of them.

steps.title: Four styles
steps.text:
- **Resources.** The API is a set of things with addresses, and a few standard methods act on them. This is the style of this course.
- **Procedures.** The API is a set of named operations that the client calls, each with its own inputs and outputs, much like calling a function. It is usually called RPC, for remote procedure call. gRPC is a widely used form of it.
- **Queries.** The API is one typed graph of data. The client sends a query that names exactly the fields it wants, and receives exactly those. GraphQL is the best known form.
- **Events.** The API is a stream of things that have happened, which the client subscribes to. Webhooks, from the last module, are the simplest form.

steps.title: What each is good at
steps.text:
| Style | Strong at | The price |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Resources | A uniform pattern that needs little explanation. Standard caching, status codes and tools. Suits third parties. | Reading a screen's worth of related data can take several requests. Operations that are not create, read, update or delete fit awkwardly. |
| Procedures | Operations that are actions. Strict typed contracts, and clients generated from them. With gRPC, compact and fast messages. | No uniform pattern, so each operation is learned on its own. Standard caching does not apply. Harder to call from a browser. |
| Queries | Many different screens, each needing a different slice of connected data, in one request. | The server becomes harder to build, to cache and to protect, because every query is different. |
| Events | Telling clients about changes as they happen. | Delivery, repeats and order all need care, and the client needs a way to catch up after a gap. |

steps.title: How to choose
steps.text:
Start with who the clients are, since the style exists to serve them.

- **Outside developers you will never meet.** Prefer resources. It is the style most people already know, and the one with the most tools.
- **Your own services calling each other.** Procedures suit this well. Both sides are yours, the operations are actions, and a typed contract catches mistakes when the code is built.
- **Several of your own apps with very different screens.** A query style can save each of them from stitching together many requests.
- **Clients that must react to changes.** Add events to whichever style you chose.

Mixtures are normal. A product can offer resources to the public, use procedures between its own services, and send events through webhooks. What matters is that each surface is consistent within itself.

steps.title: Choose a style
steps.text: Two back-end services owned by one team exchange thousands of small messages a second. Both are deployed together. The operations are things like "reserve stock" and "release stock".

steps.title: What stays the same
steps.text:
Changing the style changes the syntax. It does not remove any of the design questions.

- **Names** still have to be consistent, whether they name resources, procedures or fields in a graph.
- **Errors** still need a stable code, a readable message and a way to find the request. Some styles answer with a `200` at the HTTP level even for a failure and carry the error inside the body. The error still has to be designed.
- **Change** still has to be additive, and removals still need a schedule.
- **Retries** are still dangerous for operations that are not idempotent, so those still need a key.
- **Access** still has to be checked for every object, on every request.
- **Limits** still have to exist. A query style makes them harder, because one request can ask for very little or for a great deal.

A team that designs resources carelessly will design procedures and queries carelessly too. The discipline is the same.

steps.title: One request for everything
steps.text: A team replaces twelve resource endpoints with a single flexible query endpoint, so that any client can ask for any combination of fields and nested lists in one request.

steps.title: Exercise: three situations
steps.text:
Choose a style for each, with one sentence of reasoning.

1. The tracker opens to customers, who will write their own integrations in whatever tools they have.
2. The tracker's notification service needs to ask its user service, thousands of times a second, "which of these users want an email?".
3. A customer's reporting system has to learn within seconds that a task was completed.

Then continue.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. **Resources.** The customers are unknown, varied, and best served by the style with the lowest cost of learning and the widest tool support.
2. **Procedures.** One team owns both sides, the operation is a question with a typed answer, and speed matters more than being easy to explore.
3. **Events,** delivered by webhook, on top of the resource API. The reporting system is told when a task is completed, and it can still read the task whenever it needs the current state.

The tracker ends up offering all three, each where it fits.

questions.prompt: Which style fits best?

choices.text: Resources, because it is the most common
choices.feedback: It would work, but neither of its main strengths, wide familiarity and standard caching, is needed here.

choices.text: Procedures
choices.feedback: One team owns both ends, the operations are actions, and a typed, compact call suits a high volume of small messages.

choices.text: Events only
choices.feedback: Reserving stock needs an answer: did it work? An event stream alone does not give one.

questions.prompt: What new problem has the team taken on?

choices.text: Limits and caching, because every request is now different
choices.feedback: One query may be trivial and the next enormous. The server needs a way to measure and bound the cost of a query before running it.

choices.text: Clients can no longer choose which fields they get
choices.feedback: They can. That is what the query style offers.

choices.text: Nothing, because one endpoint is always simpler than twelve
choices.feedback: Simpler to list, harder to protect. The twelve endpoints each had a known cost.

lessons.title: Describe and review an API
lessons.intro: An API that cannot be understood from its description will be used wrongly, or not at all. The description is part of the product, and writing it early is one of the best ways to find design problems. This module covers what a description must contain, a standard format for it, and how to review a design before anyone builds it.

steps.title: Three kinds of description
steps.text:
People come to an API's description with different questions, and one document rarely answers them all.

- **A reference** lists everything: each endpoint, each field, each error. It has to be complete and exact. People look things up in it.
- **Guides** explain how to get a job done from start to finish: create a project, add tasks, receive an event when one is completed. People read these first.
- **Examples** are real requests and real responses that can be copied. Most developers start by copying one.

If only one of the three can be done well, make it the examples. A correct example answers questions the prose forgot to cover.

steps.title: What every endpoint needs
steps.text:
For each operation, a client developer needs to be able to find:

1. What it is for, in one sentence.
2. The method and the address.
3. Every parameter and field: its name, its type, whether it is required, its limits and its default.
4. A complete example request and the response to it.
5. Every error it can return, with the code and what the client should do about it.
6. The permission it needs.
7. Whether it is safe to retry, and which limits apply.

Items 5 to 7 are the ones most often left out. They are also the ones a client cannot find out by trying, because failures and limits do not show up in a quick test.

steps.title: A description a program can read
steps.text:
For HTTP APIs there is a standard format for the reference, called **OpenAPI**. It is a text file that lists the addresses, methods, parameters, bodies and responses in a fixed structure.

Because a program can read it, one file can produce the reference pages, generate client code, drive a fake server for clients to build against, and check that the real server still answers as described.

It also makes **design first** practical. Write the description before the code, share it, and argue about it while changing it still costs nothing. That is the cheapest moment the first module talked about.

steps.title: A reference entry
steps.text: This is the complete entry for one endpoint in an API's reference.

steps.title: Write the rules down once
steps.text:
Consistency across an API comes from decisions that are made once and recorded. A short **style guide** holds them. It is for the people who add endpoints, and it settles questions before they are argued again.

A useful guide fits on a page or two and answers:

- How are addresses and fields named?
- Which methods and status codes are used, and for what?
- What does every error look like?
- How do lists page, filter and sort?
- How are dates, money and identifiers written?
- How are changes made, and how is something retired?
- How does a caller prove who it is?

Each module of this course has been one section of such a guide.

steps.title: Review before building
steps.text:
A design review is a short meeting, or a written exchange, in which someone who did not write the design reads it as a client would. It needs the description and a list of questions.

The list in the example is a starting point. It is one question for each module of this course. A design that passes all of them is not guaranteed to be good, but one that fails several will cause trouble that is expensive to repair later.

steps.title: When to review
steps.text: A team has two weeks to add time tracking to the tracker's API.

steps.title: Exercise: describe one endpoint
steps.text:
Write the reference entry for `POST /projects/{id}/tasks`, which creates a task in a project. Use plain words, not OpenAPI.

Cover the seven items from earlier in this module. Invent sensible limits where you need them. Then continue.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text: The entry answers the questions a client developer would otherwise have to find out by experiment or by asking. In particular it says what each failure means and what to do about it, and that the request can be retried with a key.

questions.prompt: What is the most important thing missing?

choices.text: A longer introduction
choices.feedback: More prose would not tell the client what it needs to build against.

choices.text: The name of the programmer to contact
choices.feedback: Useful, perhaps, but a client should not need to ask a person how an endpoint behaves.

choices.text: The fields, an example, and what can go wrong
choices.feedback: Without the body's fields, an example and the errors, a client can only guess, and it will find the failures in production.

questions.prompt: When is the best time to review the design?

choices.text: In the first days, from a written description, before any code
choices.feedback: Changing a description costs minutes. The review can then shape what gets built.

choices.text: After the code is finished and tested
choices.feedback: By then a design problem means rewriting code, and there is pressure to release it as it is.

choices.text: After release, once customers give feedback
choices.feedback: After release, every fix is a breaking change or a permanent workaround.

lessons.title: Review and design a whole API
lessons.intro: This last module has no new ideas. It asks you to use the earlier ones twice: first to review an API that somebody else designed, and then to design a small one yourself from a short brief. Both are done on paper. Reading the worked answers can explain an approach, but the value is in making the attempt first.

steps.title: How to use this module
steps.text:
There are two exercises. Each one has a page that sets the task and a page that gives one possible answer.

Give each a real attempt before reading on. Twenty minutes for the review and forty for the design is about right. Write your answers down, because a design that only exists in your head has not been tested.

The checklist from the last module is repeated here to work from.

steps.title: Exercise 1: review this API
steps.text:
A small company has published this API for its task tracker. Read it as a client developer who has to build against it.

Find at least eight problems. For each, say which principle it breaks and what you would change. Then continue.

steps.title: One possible review
steps.text:
There are more than eight. These are the ones that would hurt clients soonest.

1. **Verbs in addresses, and no pattern.** `getAllTasks`, `task/create`, `deleteTask`. Use `/tasks` and `/tasks/{id}` with methods.
2. **A `GET` that deletes.** Anything that fetches links will delete tasks. Use `DELETE /tasks/{id}`.
3. **The list has no page size.** It returns every task and will fail as data grows. Add `limit` and a cursor, and return an object, not a bare list.
4. **Creating answers `200` with no address.** Answer `201` with a `Location` header.
5. **Errors return `200`.** Clients, caches and monitoring will all read failures as successes. Use the 4xx and 5xx families.
6. **The error is a sentence and leaks a query.** Give a stable code, a field, a message and a request identifier, and keep the query in the logs.
7. **The key is in the address.** It will be written to every log. Use the `Authorization` header.
8. **Field names follow no rule.** `ID`, `task_title`, `dueDate`, `Done`. Choose one style.
9. **Types that will be misread.** A date as `3/1/25`, an identifier as a number, a status as `1`. Use ISO 8601 dates, text identifiers and named values.
10. **The update replaces everything through `POST`.** Use `PATCH` for a partial change, and let clients send a version to avoid overwriting each other.
11. **Nothing can be retried safely.** Creating a task twice makes two. Accept an idempotency key.
12. **No version and no way to change.** Start at version 1 and state what clients must tolerate.

None of these needs new technology to fix. Each is a decision that was not made on purpose.

steps.title: The most urgent fix
steps.text: The company can only fix one thing before its next customer starts building.

steps.title: Exercise 2: design time tracking
steps.text:
The tracker is adding time tracking. This is the brief.

- A user records a **time entry** against a task: a date, a number of minutes, and an optional note.
- A user can change or remove their own entries. Nobody can change another person's.
- A project manager wants the total time for each task of a project, for a given week.
- The phone app is often on a poor connection.
- A customer's payroll system reads all new entries once a night.

Design the API. Cover the resources and their addresses, the methods, the JSON for one entry, what happens when input is wrong, how lists are read, how the phone app and the payroll system are kept safe, who may do what, and how the design could grow. Then continue.

steps.title: One possible design: resources and bodies
steps.text:
A time entry belongs to a task, so it is created under the task. It has its own identity, so it is read, changed and removed at its own short address. The weekly totals are a computed resource under the project.

The entry uses the conventions of the rest of the API. The identifiers are text. The day is a calendar date, because an entry has no time of day. The duration says its unit in its name. The author is a small object, and the timestamps end in `_at`.

steps.title: One possible design: behavior
steps.text:
**Wrong input** gets `422` with the usual error body, naming each field: minutes must be from 1 to 1440, and the date must be real and not in the future.

**Lists** are paged with a cursor and can be filtered by date. The payroll system asks for entries created after the last moment it saw, with `created_after`, and follows the cursor until it is `null`. It does not need a webhook, because it runs once a night.

**The phone app** sends an idempotency key with each new entry, so that a retry after a lost reply does not record the time twice. Changes are sent with `If-Match`, so that an edit made on another device is not overwritten silently.

**Access.** Recording time needs the scope `time:write`, and reading needs `time:read`. Beyond the scope, every change or removal checks that the entry belongs to the caller, and answers `403` otherwise. Reading the totals checks that the caller may see the project.

**Growth.** The response is an object, so fields such as a billable flag can be added later. The set of filters can grow. The totals resource takes its week as a parameter, so other periods can be added without a new address.

steps.title: One last judgement
steps.text: The team considers letting the client send the total directly: `PUT /tasks/42/time` with the total number of minutes for the task, instead of separate entries.

steps.title: What to take with you
steps.text:
The ideas of this course reduce to a few habits.

1. **Design from the client's side.** Write the requests and responses before the code.
2. **Be consistent.** One way to name, one way to page, one shape for errors.
3. **Keep the promises of the protocol.** Safe methods read. Status codes tell the truth.
4. **Make failure usable.** A stable code, a field, a way to find the request, and whether to retry.
5. **Assume retries and collisions.** Give creates a key and updates a version.
6. **Grow by adding.** Remove only on a published schedule.
7. **Check access for every object.** Give each credential the least it needs.
8. **Set limits and publish them.**
9. **Describe it, and have someone else read the description** before it is built.

When a new situation comes up that this course did not cover, the first habit is the one to fall back on: ask who is calling, what they are trying to do, and what they need to know when it does not work.

questions.prompt: Which fix matters most to make first?

choices.text: Renaming the fields to one style
choices.feedback: Inconsistent names are a nuisance and will be costly to change later, but they do not destroy data.

choices.text: The `GET` that deletes, and the key in the address
choices.feedback: One lets ordinary software delete tasks by fetching a link. The other writes every customer's key into logs. Both cause harm that cannot be undone.

choices.text: Adding a version number
choices.feedback: A version helps with later changes. It does nothing about the damage the current design can do today.

questions.prompt: What would be lost by storing only a total for each task?

choices.text: Nothing. It is simpler and holds the same information
choices.feedback: A single total cannot say who worked, or on which day.

choices.text: Only the notes
choices.feedback: The notes go, but so do the date and the person for each piece of work.

choices.text: Who worked when, which the weekly report and payroll both need
choices.feedback: The brief asks for totals by week and for entries that belong to a user. A bare total cannot answer either, and two people saving at once would overwrite each other.
